clue.text: Low haunts for a rich man

definitions.meaning: in the Bible parable of the rich man and Lazarus

explanation.surface: Where a wealthy man goes slumming.
explanation.definitionFit: Seedy drinking dens are called by this word, and it is also the traditional name of the wealthy man in Luke's parable.

clue.text: Stupid Daisy's body builders

parts.note: dumb means stupid in casual speech
Daisy Bell is the girl in the old music-hall song 'Daisy, Daisy' about a bicycle made for two; the possessive gives the surname plus S

explanation.surface: A dim-witted girl's muscle men.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Daisy Bell' is an 1892 music-hall song ('Daisy, Daisy, give me your answer do'). 'body builders' are weights that build muscle.
explanation.definitionFit: Hand weights used in exercise build up the muscles, so they are builders of the body.

clue.text: Tend to get the edge

definitions.meaning: to ... on or towards something is to tend towards it
the border or margin, such as a grass strip by a road

explanation.surface: Look after someone to gain an advantage.
explanation.definitionFit: Inclining towards something is to tend that way, and a border strip or margin is the other sense.

clue.text: Hull should always be in this condition

definitions.text: Hull should always be in this condition

parts.words: Hull should always be in this condition
parts.note: a ship's body ought to be neat and in good order; Hull is also a port city in Yorkshire

explanation.surface: The Yorkshire city of Hull ought to stay tidy.
explanation.walkthrough: Hull is an English port, and a hull is the body of a ship; both should be in trim, seaworthy order.
explanation.definitionFit: This means trim and in good order, as a well-kept vessel should be.

clue.text: A hot time for Robespierre

parts.note: a summer month of the French Revolutionary calendar, named from the Greek for heat, in which Robespierre fell

explanation.surface: Robespierre had a rough summer.
explanation.walkthrough: The Revolutionary calendar named its months after the seasons; this one's name comes from the Greek for heat, and it saw the coup of 1794 that toppled Robespierre.
explanation.definitionFit: This was the eleventh month of the French Revolutionary calendar, its name meaning heat, when Robespierre was overthrown and executed.

clue.text: It was well-drawn in "Alice"

parts.note: in the Mad Hatter's tea party the Dormouse tells of three sisters living at the bottom of a well who drew a sticky syrup from it

explanation.surface: A good illustration in a children's book.
explanation.walkthrough: 'well-drawn' suggests a fine illustration, but means drawn up from a well: the Dormouse's tale in Alice's Adventures in Wonderland.
explanation.definitionFit: Golden syrup's darker cousin is what the Dormouse's sisters drew from their well in Lewis Carroll's story.

clue.text: What the rich are landed with

definitions.text: What the rich are landed with

parts.words: What the rich are landed with
parts.note: wealthy landowners possess large country properties; landed also means saddled with

explanation.surface: Wealthy people's burden.
explanation.walkthrough: 'landed with' suggests being stuck with a burden, but the landed gentry own large properties.
explanation.definitionFit: Large country properties are what wealthy landed families own.

clue.text: By gum, it's held tight at the back !

definitions.text: By gum, it's held tight at the back !

parts.words: By gum, it's held tight at the back !
parts.note: a back grinding tooth is held firmly in place by the gum; 'By gum!' is also a northern English exclamation

explanation.surface: A northern exclamation about something gripped firmly behind.
explanation.walkthrough: 'By gum!' is a Yorkshire exclamation of surprise; here it is literal, the gum around a back tooth.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a back grinding tooth, rooted firmly in the gum at the rear of the jaw.

clue.text: Converted to a divine unorthodoxy

indicators.note: converted says the letters are changed into a different form

explanation.surface: A religious convert turns heretic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Converted' looks religious beside 'divine' but signals the anagram of TO A DIVINE.
explanation.definitionFit: Departing from accepted belief or practice is a deviation, which is what unorthodoxy means.

clue.text: Truly this is a test of sobriety

definitions.text: Truly this is a test of sobriety

parts.words: Truly this is a test of sobriety
parts.note: the tongue-twister 'truly ...' is hard to say after a few drinks

explanation.surface: A real check on whether someone is drunk.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Truly' looks like an adverb, but it is the first half of the tongue-twister 'truly rural', a traditional test of drunkenness.
explanation.definitionFit: Saying 'truly' followed by this countryside word is a famously hard tongue-twister for anyone who has been drinking.

clue.text: Fun resulting from the Mikado's penal reforms

definitions.text: Fun resulting from the Mikado's penal reforms

parts.words: Fun resulting from the Mikado's penal reforms
parts.note: in Gilbert and Sullivan's opera the Mikado sings of making each punishment fit the crime, calling the result a source of innocent fun

explanation.surface: A Japanese emperor's prison policy proves amusing.
explanation.walkthrough: In The Mikado, the song 'A more humane Mikado' ends with the punishment fitting the crime, 'a source of innocent merriment'.
explanation.definitionFit: Merriment is another word for fun, and it is the word the Mikado's song uses for what his punishments produce.

clue.text: Goldsmith has no love for this bird

indicators.note: has no says the letter for love is taken away from the writer's first name

parts.note: Oliver Goldsmith, the eighteenth-century Irish writer
love is zero in tennis, written as the letter O

explanation.surface: A writer has no affection for a certain bird.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Goldsmith' looks like a jeweller but is Oliver Goldsmith. The liver bird is the mythical cormorant-like emblem of Liverpool.
explanation.definitionFit: The liver bird is the legendary seabird that stands as the symbol of the city of Liverpool.

clue.text: Sober robes might doubly become them

indicators.note: the letters can be rearranged into the answer, and doubly signals that the next word can be too

explanation.surface: Sombre garments would suit some people twice over.
explanation.walkthrough: Both 'Sober' and 'robes' are anagrams of the answer, hence 'doubly'; 'them' is the people meant. The Boers were Dutch-descended settlers in southern Africa, known for plain, sober dress.
explanation.definitionFit: Them refers to the people meant: the Dutch-descended farmers of South Africa, whose name is an anagram of each word.

clue.text: Provide universal law reform — what a scream!

parts.note: to cater is to provide food or what is needed

indicators.note: reform says the letters are reshaped into a new order

parts.note: U is the film-certificate abbreviation for universal

explanation.surface: Arranging a sweeping legal reform makes someone shriek.
explanation.walkthrough: 'reform' rearranges U and LAW into WAUL. 'scream' looks like a joke but is literal: a cat's howl.
explanation.definitionFit: A caterwaul is a shrill wailing howl like a cat's, which is just what a scream is.

clue.text: What will ruin the lake, given time

definitions.text: What will ruin the lake, given time

indicators.note: will ruin says the letters of the following word are wrecked into a new order

parts.note: an age is a long period of time

explanation.surface: Something that spoils a lake if left long enough.
explanation.walkthrough: 'will ruin' scrambles LAKE into LEAK, then AGE (time) follows. The whole clue also defines it: escaping water spoils a lake.
explanation.definitionFit: Water escaping steadily would empty and spoil a lake over a long period, so the whole clue describes it.

clue.text: Here craft is in evidence still

definitions.text: Here craft is in evidence still

parts.words: Here craft is in evidence still
parts.note: boats are moored motionless in a sheltered spot where ships drop their hooks

explanation.surface: Traditional skill can still be seen in this place.
explanation.walkthrough: 'craft' suggests skill, but means boats; 'still' means motionless, not 'yet'.
explanation.definitionFit: A harbour area where ships drop their hook and lie at rest, so vessels are seen there unmoving.

clue.text: Navigational difficulties

parts.note: narrow sea channels are hard for a ship to get through, and the same word means difficulties, as in dire trouble

explanation.surface: Trouble steering a ship.
explanation.definitionFit: Narrow channels between seas are hazards for shipping, and the word also means a hard situation, as in 'dire'.

clue.text: Revolutionary clubmen ?

parts.note: members of the service clubs named after rotation, whose emblem is a wheel

explanation.surface: Members of a radical political society.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Revolutionary' suggests rebels, but means turning: Rotary International's emblem is a wheel and meetings once rotated between members' offices.
explanation.definitionFit: Members of Rotary International, a service club whose name comes from rotating, belong to clubs.

clue.text: He goes after gold, winning first place

indicators.note: first place says the word for winning comes before the heraldic gold

parts.note: winning is success
OR is gold in heraldry

explanation.surface: An athlete chases a gold medal and takes the top spot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'gold' and 'first place' paint a race; OR is the heraldic word for gold.
explanation.definitionFit: One who follows on after another in a role or position goes after the previous holder.

clue.text: Conceal city district in a maze of trees

indicators.note: in places the postal district inside the scrambled trees
a maze of says the letters of the trees are twisted into a jumble

parts.note: EC is the London postal district covering the City

explanation.surface: Hiding a part of town inside a wooded labyrinth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a maze of' rearranges TREES to SRETE, and 'in' puts EC inside it after the S.
explanation.definitionFit: To secrete something is to hide it away, a synonym of conceal.

clue.text: Unable to gaze in Gaza

parts.note: Milton's blinded Samson was '... in Gaza', later the title of an Aldous Huxley novel

explanation.surface: Someone can't see in a Middle Eastern city.
explanation.walkthrough: Milton's Samson Agonistes describes the blinded Samson as 'Eyeless in Gaza'.
explanation.definitionFit: Without sight, a person cannot gaze; Milton used the phrase of Samson at Gaza.

clue.text: Radiant start of play, ending not quite nice

parts.note: a play's first section is Act I

indicators.note: not quite says the printed word is short of its final letter

explanation.surface: A drama begins brightly but finishes a touch unpleasantly.
explanation.definitionFit: Actinic describes radiation, especially light able to cause chemical change, so it means radiant.

clue.text: Caster's problem ?

parts.note: a casting director must find the right female performer for a part

explanation.surface: Trouble for someone throwing a fishing line.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Caster' suggests an angler or a sugar caster, but here is a casting director choosing a performer.
explanation.definitionFit: A female stage or screen player is who a casting director has to find for a part.

clue.text: Good prospects for the ancient mariner here

definitions.text: Good prospects for the ancient mariner here

parts.words: Good prospects for the ancient mariner here
parts.note: the lookout's platform at the top of a sailing ship's mast gives the widest view to an old sailor

explanation.surface: A place where an old sailor's future looks bright.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Good prospects' looks like career hopes, but means fine views from the masthead lookout post.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the lookout platform high on a ship's mast, where a sailor gets the widest view of the sea.

clue.text: But as trainee he may not have an older brother

definitions.text: But as trainee he may not have an older brother

parts.words: But as trainee he may not have an older brother
parts.note: the word means a younger son, yet as an officer trainee the holder need not be a younger son

explanation.surface: A trainee might be an only or eldest child.
explanation.walkthrough: The word's old sense is a younger son, who by definition has an older brother; in its trainee sense he need not.
explanation.definitionFit: This is both a younger son of a family and a young military trainee.

clue.text: Moving this case for a rise

definitions.text: Moving this case for a rise

parts.words: Moving this case for a rise
parts.note: add the word case to get a flight of steps; a moving one is an escalator, and a single step is a rise

explanation.surface: Shifting a suitcase to get a pay increase.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Moving this case' reads as shifting luggage; but this word plus 'case' moving is an escalator, and the word alone is a single step up.
explanation.definitionFit: A single step is a rise, and with 'case' it makes a flight of steps that can move.

clue.text: Plunder the old brigade went after

definitions.meaning: to ... a place is to ransack or plunder it
the old British regiment was called the ... Brigade, so the word 'Brigade' came after this one

explanation.surface: Veterans chased off with the loot.
explanation.definitionFit: Ransacking is to plunder, and the old British Army regiment was the Rifle Brigade, the word Brigade following it.

clue.text: Inordinate increase in the water 'rate

parts.note: an overflow of water over dry land is an excessive rise in water level, punning on a utility bill

explanation.surface: An outrageous hike in the water charge.
explanation.walkthrough: 'water rate' looks like a utility bill, but means the level of water rising out of control.
explanation.definitionFit: A deluge is a huge overflow of water over normally dry land.

clue.text: In retrospect, she is helpful

indicators.note: in retrospect means looking back, so the phrase is read from end to start

parts.note: something that is helpful is an aid

explanation.surface: Looking back, a woman was a great help.
explanation.walkthrough: 'is helpful' gives AN AID; 'In retrospect' reads it backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Diana is a woman's name, so it is a she.

clue.text: They have their ups and downs in the States

definitions.text: They have their ups and downs in the States

parts.words: They have their ups and downs in the States
parts.note: the American word for lifts, which carry people up and down floors of a building

explanation.surface: Americans go through good times and bad.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ups and downs' suggests fortunes, but is literal: the American term for lifts.
explanation.definitionFit: Americans call lifts by this word, and lifts travel up and down all day.

clue.text: The opposition leader gets …up and speculates

indicators.note: leader picks the opening letter of the word opposition

parts.note: to get up from bed or a seat is to rise, so he rises

explanation.surface: The head of the opposition stands up and guesses about the future.
explanation.walkthrough: 'speculates' is a verb, so the answer must be THEORISES; THEORISTS as filed matches the crossing letters but not the clue.
explanation.definitionFit: To theorise is to form ideas without proof, which is what speculating means.

clue.text: Man's episcopal associate

parts.note: the Isle of Man shares its Church of England diocese with another name, the bishop being 'of ... and Man'

explanation.surface: A fellow cleric of some person.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Man' looks like a person, but is the Isle of Man: its bishop is the Bishop of Sodor and Man.
explanation.definitionFit: The Church of England diocese of the Isle of Man is called Sodor and Man, so this name is linked to Man in the bishop's title.
